analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share parts, tools, and repair manuals with independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House subcommittee and died when the 118th Congress ended, without a committee vote or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Repair Act would require makers of digital electronics — phones, laptops, appliances, farm machinery — to sell replacement parts and repair tools, and share service manuals and schematics, with independent repair shops and device owners on the same terms they give their own authorized repair shops. It would also ban 'parts pairing' tricks that disable a device or show fake warnings when an independent part is installed. Enforcement would fall to the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general. The bill never got past a House subcommittee before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Device owners, independent repair shops, and users of electronics-heavy machinery such as farm equipment. They gain the legal right to buy parts, tools, and repair documentation at the same prices the manufacturer offers its own authorized shops, plus bans on software locks that degrade a device after third-party repair. That means lower repair costs, more repair options, and less pressure to replace a broken device with a new one.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners 'on fair and reasonable terms', defined as no worse than the best terms offered to authorized repair providers [S2].
The bill bans parts pairing practices that block functional third-party parts, degrade performance after independent repair, trigger false warnings, or add fees for future repairs [S2].

Even devices with security locks must be repairable: makers must provide what is needed to disable and reset the lock, though trade secrets are protected and the bill does not cover cars or medical devices [S2].
The FTC enforces violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue for injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers of digital electronics, who would lose pricing and control advantages over the repair market and bear the cost of supplying parts, tools, and documentation to outside shops on equal terms.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers argue that mandated repair tools and forced disabling of security locks can create security and liability risks; the bill responds by protecting trade secrets but still requires makers to supply what is needed to defeat electronic security locks [S2].

The bill exempts motor vehicles and medical devices entirely, so the two sectors where repair restrictions have drawn the most attention — car dealerships and hospital equipment — are outside its reach [S2].
The scope covers any product with embedded digital electronics, a broad reach that imposes ongoing compliance costs on manufacturers of everything from appliances to toys [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers — cheaper, faster repairs and less forced device replacement — are concrete and the compliance costs to manufacturers are real but modest for companies of that scale. The biggest honest criticisms are the security-lock provision and the large carve-outs for cars and medical devices, which keep the most consequential repair monopolies untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat at subcommittee from its referral in May 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025; the committee never acted on it.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Morelle introduced the bill with Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez as cosponsor in May 2024 [S1].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, a week later, to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
No further action was taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and equipment manufacturers keep their repair monopoly — controlling who can fix their devices, at what price, and with which parts — and device owners continue to face high repair costs and pressure to replace rather than repair.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Electronics manufacturers kept their repair control

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — one Democratic sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors — so the bill never drew a bipartisan coalition that might have forced committee action.

industries.note: The bill would end their control over the repair market: they would have to sell parts, tools, and documentation to independent shops and owners at no worse terms than they give authorized shops, and could no longer use parts pairing to degrade third-party repairs. Their gain from the status quo is device owners' cost.
The bill's core beneficiaries alongside device owners: they would get legal access to parts, tools, and manuals needed to compete with manufacturer-authorized repair networks.

Tractors and other farm machinery are digital electronic equipment and not excluded by the bill's motor vehicle carve-out, so makers of heavily computerized farm equipment would face the same repair information and anti-parts-pairing duties — a sector where farmers have complained of long, costly dealer-only repairs.
